articleTitle: A parallel processing tutorial
abstract: An overview of parallel computing is provided, with reference to numerical analysis and, in particular, to computational electromagnetics. The history of parallelism is reviewed, and the general principles are provided. The two main types of parallelism encountered, pipelining and replication are discussed, and an example of each is described. A parallel algorithm for forming a matrix-vector product is presented and analyzed. This is then used as the core of a parallel conjugate gradient algorithm. The theoretically predicted efficiency and the measured efficiency are compared. A glossary and a brief discussion of the available literature on parallel processing are included.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Simplified calculation of coverage area for MF AM broadcast stations
abstract: It is shown that the coverage area of medium- and high-frequency stations using ground-wave propagation beyond the horizon, especially MF AM stations, can be calculated by a simplified method. Recent field measurements have shown that the cumbersome FCC and CCIR calculations for estimating service area can be simplified to allow calculations with a PC, or even a programmable pocket calculator. The ground-wave electrical field intensity calculations are simplified by the introduction of a shadow or diffraction factor in the Norton planar earth expression. This factor permits the ground E field to be calculated well beyond the geometric and radio horizon, where E-field values are close to the atmospheric noise level. The approach permits engineers or technicians to calculate their own E=field curves for any frequency and any kind of soil.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: The Electromagnetic Code Consortium
abstract: A decision was made in 1987 to consolidate radar cross section (RCS) code development sponsored by the US armed services and NASA. An RCS Code Consortium was formed, consisting of a government steering group and members from the industrial/academic community. Since the formation of the Consortium, significant progress has been made to advance code development work sponsored by the US government. This paper is intended to make the RCS community aware of the Electromagnetic Code Consortium, so that potential contributors to code development can become involved with its work. It covers the approach taken by the Consortium, the acquisition of a government-owned geometry code, validation, language and documentation, the support contractor, a survey of industry codes, and benchmarking.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Optimum tilt for elevation-scanned phased arrays
abstract: It is shown that, subject to certain restrictions, the optimum tilt angle can be calculated as a function of only the highest beam elevation angle. The term optimum means the condition that the antenna gain at the horizon is maximum. The restrictions are that the antenna be operated outside the grating-lobe regime for all required scan angles and that scan angles greater than 60 degrees off broadside by avoided to allow useful operation of the radar system (considering antenna impedance match, sidelobes, gain, and beam width). It is assumed that the antenna, in principle, can be impedance matched to any elevation angle, leaving the match at broadside as a special case, without particular advantages. The results indicate that for most practical requirements (high-beam elevation between 45 degrees and 70 degrees ) the optimum tilt angle should be around 20 degrees to 30 degrees .<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Alignment fixture for millimeter waveguide
abstract: An alignment fixture for handling the precise waveguide connection procedures required in performing gain measurements of millimeter-wave antennas is described. Two versions of the fixture were developed: one for small devices, such as standard gain horns, which can be supported by the fixture, and another for larger devices. These systems, along with a properly-installed flange, can reduce the measurement uncertainty associated with the connection from greater than 1 dB to a few hundredths of a decibel. For measurements in the WR-22 and WR-15 waveguide bands, the overall gain error for millimeter-frequency antenna measurements has decreased from 0.31 dB to 0.10 dB.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Comments on 'The role of analysis in an age of computers: view from the analytical side'
abstract: The commenter disagrees with the implication in the above-titled paper by R.E. Collin (ibid., vol.32, p.27-31 (Aug. 1990)) that analytical solutions are the only way, or even the best way, to check the accuracy of numerical solutions. He expresses surprise that no mention was made of verifying solutions accuracy by comparison with measured data. He argues that measurements provide what is often the best way of verifying the accuracy of a solution to a practical problem in electromagnetics, regardless of the extent to which the solution is analytical or numerical. He gives an example from the paper (radiation conductance of an open-ended microstrip line versus substrate thickness) to illustrate this point.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: A view of teaching electromagnetism to undergraduates in Karlsruhe, FRG
abstract: The teaching of electromagnetism in the electrical engineering department at Karlsruhe is described. In the first two years of undergraduate studies, static electromagnetic problems are dealt with in courses on the basics of electricity. The students then take an interim examination, fairly well comparable to the bachelor's. Following this examination, the students have to pass compulsory lectures, after which they can specialize in one of fourteen areas. Three of these deal primarily with electromagnetism: theoretical electrotechnology; RF and microwaves; and optical communication. For nearly all lectures, the professors write their own textbooks, but a number of well-recognized international books are also recommended.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: The measurements column (antenna gain measurement)
abstract: Four different methods for measuring the gain of circularly polarized antennas under test are presented. Errors that result from these measurements are discussed. The errors presented would form part of an overall error budget analysis.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: The impedance matrix localization (IML) method for moment-method calculations
abstract: The impedance matrix localization (IML) method, a modification of the standard method of moments that can be implemented as a modification to existing computer programs, is examined. This modification greatly eases the excessive storage requirements and long computation times of moment-method approaches by using novel bases and testing function that localize the important interactions to only a small number of elements within the impedance matrix elements can be made so small (typically 10/sup -4/ to 10/sup -6/ in relative magnitude) that they may be approximated by zero. In the case of a two-dimensional body with unknowns on its surface, both analytical arguments and numerical calculations suggest that, for an N*N matrix, about 100N matrix elements will need to be kept, even for very large N. The resulting sparse matrix requires storage for only 100N complex numbers rather than for N/sup 2/ numbers. Similar results are expected in three dimensions. The structure of the resulting matrix problem allows the use of highly efficient solution methods. Results are given for one such possibility: iteration preconditioned by incomplete LU decomposition.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Origin and development of the method of moments for field computation
abstract: A short history is given of the development of mathematical methods related to the method of moments and used for electromagnetic field computations. A brief description of the general theory is given, emphasizing various viewpoints which lead to different names given to the method. Its relationships to the Rayleigh-Ritz variational method and to the perturbation method are shown and discussed.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Array feeds for reflector surface distortion compensation: concepts and implementation
abstract: The development of a compensation algorithm based on the use of array feeds and a focal-plane conjugate field approach is discussed. Results of numerical simulations performed to verify the accuracy of the computer programs are examined, and an experimental study is described. Both the numerical and experimental results show that the array will compensate for the slowly varying surface distortion. In particular, for some typical, slowly varying thermal or gravitational surface distortions, a 19-element array feed can improve the reflector performance considerably. Additionally, it is demonstrated that it will be possible to compensate for the surface distortion without actual knowledge of the distortion itself.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: AVNA-based polarimetric scatterometers
abstract: The polarization synthesis technique for measuring the scattering properties of point and distributed targets is discussed, and it is pointed out that accurate measurements of both the magnitude and phase of the scattered signal are now possible by using the signal-processing and error-correction techniques of the automatic vector network analyzer (AVNA). The principles of operation of the AVNA are given, and an overview of AVNA-based scatterometer configurations in use today at centimeter and millimeter wavelengths is provided.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: On the implementation of the conjugate gradient Fourier transform method for scattering by planar plates
abstract: The accuracy of two conjugate gradient fast Fourier transform formulations for computing the electromagnetic scattering by resistive plates of an arbitrary periphery is discussed. One of the formulations is based on a discretization of the integral equations prior to the introduction of the Fourier transform, whereas the other is based on a similar discretization after the introduction of the Fourier transform. The efficiency and accuracy of these formulations are examined by comparison with measured data for rectangular and nonrectangular plates. The latter method is found to provide a more accurate computation of the plate scattering by eliminating aliasing errors (other than those due to undersampling). It is also found to be substantially more efficient. Its greatest advantage is realized when solving large systems generated by convolutional operators not yielding Toeplitz matrices, as is the case with plates having nonuniform resistivity.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Diffraction: the first recorded observation
abstract: The discovery of diffraction by Francesco Maria Grimaldi is described. He described the experiments that led to its discovery in the book De Lumine, first published in 1665, two years after Grimaldi's death. Grimaldi's life and his experimental observations are described. Newton's disregard of Grimaldi's work and substitution of the word inflexion for diffraction are discussed.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: A survey of the effects of reflector surface distortions on sidelobe levels
abstract: A survey of the literature relating to the effects of reflector surface distortions is presented, with particular attention to the Zernike-mode method of describing distortions and calculating the resultant radiation patterns. The errors are classified on the basis of whether they are random or systematic, since that is what determines the method of treatment. Systematic errors are further classified as periodic or nonperiodic. The results of studies into sidelobes generated by periodic surface distortions call into question the suitability of the current method of sidelobe envelope specification.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: High temperature superconductors and their application in passive antenna systems
abstract: The basic physics of superconductivity is reviewed and related to the high-temperature superconductors. The high-frequency characteristics of the new materials are examined, and the two-fluid model is introduced and used to derive an empirical expression for the conductivity of superconductors. The advantages and disadvantages of using these superconductors in the construction of high-frequency transmission lines and passive microwave and millimeter-wave antenna systems are discussed.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Compared broad-wall slots for array applications
abstract: An overview of the theory, properties, and potential applications of compound slots is given. Methods for analyzing compound slots are discussed. Scattering properties of the compound slot are examined, covering resonance and the equivalent circuit model, resonant length scattering in the main waveguide, the aperture electric field, and off-resonant characteristics. Array characteristics are also considered, including external mutual coupling, internal higher order mode coupling, and some factors to consider in designing array configurations. Problems remaining to be solved are indicated.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: On the relationship between the MoM and the GMT [EM theory]
abstract: The method of moments (MoM) is compared with the generalized multipole technique (GMT), which has been shown to be very efficient. Although the GMT can be considered to be a variant of the MoM, it is based on a completely different philosophical foundation. Both the foundation and concrete implementations are considered. It is shown how the MMP code, based on the GMT, can profit from MoM concepts, and how MoM codes can profit from GMT ideas.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: What's new in antennas?
abstract: Innovative designs, novelty, and creative ideas, currently reported in the international antenna literature, are highlighted in the areas of elements, traveling-wave arrays, apertures, arrays, measurements, and material development. Manufacturing and operational aspects are noted and the driving forces identified. The extent to which antenna technology is mature, the role of research, and degrees of design freedom are considered in some depth. Influences and innovation likely to be experienced within the next five years are conjectured upon, together with some speculation for the more distant future.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: PCs for AP (EM computation)
abstract: An analysis is presented of how the geometrical complexity and electrical size of modeling electromagnetic problems might be expected to increase as computation speed and storage continue to grow. It is assumed that as moderately to massively parallel computers become available, computation bandwidths of 10/sup 16//hour by 1995 and 10/sup 18//hour by the year 2000 can be anticipated. Two key questions are examined, namely how many arithmetic operations are needed to obtain the information sought and how fast these computations can be done on the computers available.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: A trilogy of antenna observations
abstract: Three observations are presented on (1) sidelobes of rectangular antennas; (2) maximum off-boresight antenna gain; and (3) antenna near-field as a function of direction.

articleTitle: Beam squint in parabolic reflector antennas with circularly polarized feeds [Antenna Designer's Notebook]
abstract: The beam squint phenomenon is an important design issue for modern reflector antennas, because it can affect the antenna pointing performance. For long-distance communications, like satellite or deep-space communications, this effect must be care- fully taken into account in order to avoid any degradation. In some design considerations, one may use the squint phenomenon to one's advantage in separating two RHC- and LHC-polarized beams. Squint was previously observed in offset parabolic reflectors with an on-focus circularly polarized feed [l], such as that shown in Figure 1. It must be emphasized that this squint only occurs for antennas with circularly polarized feed, but not for those for which the feed is linearly polarized.

articleTitle: The role of analysis in an age of computers: view from the analytical side
abstract: The role of both past and current analysis in computer-based electromagnetics research is examined. Some observations on the current status of computer-based solutions are presented. It is concluded that analysis will remain an essential tool for making discoveries of electromagnetic phenomena, for providing physical insight into complex phenomena, and for the development of robust problem formulations and numerical methods, so that computed results with verifiable accuracy can be achieved. It is also concluded that more attention to verifying the accuracy of numerical results obtained from computer solutions is needed.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: AP-S Turnstile
abstract: Many AP-S members are involved in the analysis and design of C<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</sup> systems. Now they may have to watch out for E<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</sup>! This new (?) acronym, which stands for Electromagnetic Environmental Effects, appears on the cover of the 1989 annual issue of ITEM Update, a supplement to the International Journal of EMC (published by ROBAR industries). It is interesting that whereas electrical engineers have been busy reducing their entire professional vocabulary to a string of acronyms (the centennial edition of the IEEE Standard Diruonary of Electrical and Electronics Terms lists no fewer than 15,000), the medical profession has managed to concoct the supposedly longest word in the language -- pneumonoultranicroscopicsilicovolcanoconiosis. Cited in The Oxford English Dictionary, second edition (1989, list price $2,500), the word refers to a particular lung disease [Editor's note: it also plays h.avoc with electronic publishing hyphenation algonthms! WRS]

articleTitle: Research in computational electromagnetics at the University of Michigan
abstract: The history of the Radiation Laboratory at the University of Michigan is briefly recounted, and its present composition of staff, faculty, and graduate students is described. Research in electromagnetic scattering at the laboratory is reviewed, covering high-frequency scattering and two- and three-dimensional numerical simulation. Work on passive monolithic circuits and antennas, including numerical modeling of planar discontinuities and antennas, planar discontinuities and transitions, and antenna feeding networks, is discussed.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Antenna designer's notebook-effects of a missing element on Taylor array patterns
abstract: It is well known that the sidelobe level of a tapered low-sidelobe array is degraded by a missing or failed element and that the effect is strongest (worst) when the outage (missing element) is at or near the center of the array. To illustrate this quantitatively, the effects of one missing center element in various tapered linear arrays is shown.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: The calibration horn antenna
abstract: The construction and history of the calibration horn antenna, a large standard-gain horn at the National Radio Astronomy Observatory, Green Bank, West Virginia, are discussed. Construction of the horn began in 1958. Its purpose was to make absolute measurements by observing a strong source directly with a standard-gain horn antenna. The discussion covers: the antenna design; fabricating and erecting the horn; early electronics and first results; thermal calibrations and corrections to the data; data collection and reduction related work done with the Bell Telephone Laboratories horn; measurements in 1968-78; observations at 820 MHz; comparison with the EB map; radio source Cas A flux density at 820 MHz; and interferometric measurements. The observations are summarized and discussed.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: A comparison of cloud models (EM wavescattering)
abstract: Five different cloud models are compared over a broad frequency range. They are the model of K.L. Gunn and T.W. East (1954), the model of H.J. Liebe et al. (1989), D.H. Staelin's (1966) model, S. Slobin's (1982) model, and the model of E.E. Altshuler and R. Marr (1989). A short tutorial review of the theoretical basis and limitations of each cloud model is included. It is shown that the models all tend to agree at frequencies below 40 GHz, and for light to medium cloud conditions; however, above 10 GHz and for heavy to very heavy clouds, the models diverge.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: PCs for AP
abstract: This month's column will not discuss the usual PCrelated news and topics, but will instead focus on an informal report prepared bv the ElectroMagnetic Modeling Software Commlttee after the Workshop held at the 1989 San Jose meeting. As you might have recognized, if you have read more than a few past columns, I have chosen to interpret whatever charter has been given to me by the Magazine/Newsletter Editor, Ross Stone, in the broadest possible sense. Thus, these columns have included literally anything interesting to me, which I thought might afso interest you, in either an EM, PC, or computational sense. I have much appreciated the license this has given me, and hope not to have overly abused it. Consequently, it seems to that "PCs for AP" is also an appropriate place for report.

articleTitle: Comments on "From 'Reaction Concept' to 'Conjugate Gradient': Have We Made Any Progress?" and Reply to Dr. Wang's Comments
abstract: Dr. Sarkar's paper, as the feature article of the August 1989 AP-S Newsletter [1], provides a vivid and informal (and therefore perhaps more revealing and informative) discussion on a subject of common interest. However, he has also expressed several views which, according to my observation, are not shared by many students of the field. Since Dr. Sarkar specifically referenced my work as an introductory basis for his discussions, and since he has, to some extent, misinterpreted my opinions, I would like to offer the following comments and clarifications, which hopefully will provide the readers a more clear and balanced view on this subject.

abstract: Because of pressures of new ventures, Ray King has had to resign as Chairman of the Wave Propagation Standards Committee (WPSC). Ray stepped down at the June '89 San Jose meeting, and turned the gavel over to me, Bud Flood.

abstract: I usually have a column, "From the Screen of Stone," in most issues. The range of topics for this column is wide, but most center around computer- related items of interest to electrical engineers. This is an abbreviated version of it, because of a variety of factors which combined to limit the amount of time I had to produce this issue. Please let me know what topics are of interest to you.

articleTitle: A Message from the President
abstract: When I talked to Ross Stone on December 26, he gently reminded me that one of the regular activities of an AP President is to contribute regularly to this column, and that the deadline for it to be included in the February issue was the next day! After I came up with the "very legitimate" excuse that our next AdCom meeting (and my first as the President) will not be held until January 6, he agreed that I could send in mv column no later than January 8. So, at the risk of being disorganized, here is my first contribution to this column as your new President for 1990.

articleTitle: Report on CCIR Study Group 5 final meeting
abstract: The Final Meeting, of the 1986-1990 study period of September 19 to October 5. The terms of reference of Study Group 5, was held in Geneva, Switzerland, from Study Group 5 encompass propagation in non-ionized medla, and natural radio noise above 50 MHz.

articleTitle: Further comments on the gain of active antennas and planar arrays
abstract: Editor's note: Two additional comments relating to the discussions on the definitions of gain for. active antennas and planar arrays which appeared In the October, 1989, Newsletterhave been received. The first is a short note from Palti Kirshner (Antenna 330, Ashdod 77102, Israel), who enclosed a aper (P. Department, ELTA Electronics Industries Ltd., PO Box Kirshner, "Gain Estimations in Active Phasei Arrays," digest of the Sixteenth IEEE Conference of Electr~cal and Electronics Engineers in Israel, March 7-9, 1989, Tel-Aviv, Israel, paper 2.2.8) defined and discussed the differences between the transmit gain and the receive gain in an active phased array. Kirshner goes on to write, "I would like to add that defining the active array by its directivity and EIRP was found b us useful. It is the method now used by ELTA for a8 our active phased array systems." The second comment is from J. W. Carr, 405 Rancho Arroyo Parkway, Apt. 187, Fremont, CA 94536. It appears below. WRS.

articleTitle: Editor's comments
abstract: Welcome to a new decade, and your new Magazine! We are now an official IEEE magazine - the newest one - but with one of the oldest and finest backgrounds in the IEEE. Welcome, also, to our new readers, who are now receiving us through the institutional subscriptions associated with the All Transactions Package (ATP, but better described as the "all IEEE archival periodicals" package). Institutions and non-IEEE members can also subscribe to this Magazine separately. If your institution does not get the ATP, please suggest that they subscribe to the Magazine. Information on how to do this is on page 3, below the Table of Contents. This issue carries the identification Volume 32, Number 1, for a very good reason: This is the thirty-second year of publication for the Antennas and Propagation Society. It is a tribute to the volunteers you see listed on the inside front cover, and to all of those who have supported this Magazine, and its predecessor publication, the AP-S Newsletter, for so kmg that we have achieved the status of an IEEE magazine.

articleTitle: The CAEME Column
abstract: WOW! - CAEME is now an NSF/IEEE Center for Computer Applications in Electromagnetic Education. In three short months, CAEME is a national center funded by the Undergraduate Science, Engineering, and Mathematics Division of NSF, and managed by the Executive Office of IEEE. Under this broad-based organizational arrangement, CAEME has, thus far, attracted participation by three Societies including the AP-S (host society), MIT-S, and the Applied Computational Electromagnetics Society (ACES). Hewlett-Packard decided to sponsor CAEME, and Hughes Aircraft is seriously considering joining in. Hughes actually sent an observer to Salt Lake Citv to attend the first CAEME Policy Board meeting.

articleTitle: Historical article on Lester C. Van Atta [From the Historian]
abstract: I am very pleased to present the personal history of Dr. Lester C. Van Atta. I have known Dr. Van Atta since the early 195Os, when I was a project officer in the Air Force, and visited the Hughes Laboratory at Culver City. Many of the pioneering antenna engineers in our Society worked at this laboratory during the 50s and 60s. Several of these people, who come to mind, are Bob Hansen, Monty Erlich, and Wolfgang Kummer, among many others.
